video_title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
gist: Rob Snyder (author of The Power of Pull) lays out the PULL framework (Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations) as a test for product-market fit, and walks through finding ideas via immersion, cold outreach, discovery calls, closing, retention and a 'case study factory' model. He argues against design partners and pilots and for selling to learn.

insights.claim: Rob Snyder defines pull as a person who would be weird not to buy: someone with a project on their to-do list they are trying to complete right now but cannot with existing tools, methods or options, making them like a coiled spring.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Replaces vague pain-point and value-prop screens with a concrete test of buyer state.
insights.quote: it's about priorities a certain kind of priority where somebody's trying to do something they got a project on their to-do list

insights.claim: The pull acronym has four required parts: Project on the to-do list, Unavoidable right now, List of options considered, and Limitations that make those options not good enough; all four must be present at once.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: A four-box checklist founders can fill out per prospect to diagnose why a deal stalls.

insights.claim: Missing elements produce predictable behavior: project without unavoidability or with inadequate limitations yields complaining but no buying, and if existing options are good enough the buyer says they will handle it with tools they already have.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Diagnoses whether a lukewarm response is a timing problem or an alternatives problem.

insights.claim: Pull belongs to a person, not a company: you sell to the head of legal at SpaceX or an operating partner at a PE firm with a specific stuck project, not to the account or segment.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: ICPs defined at company or segment level hide the real buyer and mislead outreach.
insights.quote: One of the main mistakes people make is thinking that pull is a thing that a company has. It's a thing a person has.

insights.claim: Pull exists before and independent of the founder, so the job is to find it rather than convince people to want the product; Snyder says convincing is very hard if possible at all.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Reframes go-to-market from persuasion to search, reducing founder self-blame.

insights.claim: Traditional PMF criteria (hair-on-fire pain, differentiated solution, real value, daily-use design partners) failed Snyder's own startup for two years, because people can agree a product solves pain and still not drop priorities to buy it.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Pain and value are necessary but not sufficient signals of demand.

insights.claim: Jump, an AI note-taker for financial advisors, illustrates full pull: advisors must take notes and enter them in a CRM or risk legal trouble, and generic AI note-takers failed on CRM integration and SEC compliance uncertainty, so the product was ripped out of their hands.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Compliance and integration gaps are what turn a crowded category into pull.

insights.claim: The same note-taking pitch to insurance agents failed Jump's test because the unavoidable element was missing (they are not required to put notes into a CRM) and their existing option of not taking notes was fine.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Adjacent segments with the same surface pain can lack the force that creates urgency.

insights.claim: Use the pull framework upstream of product ideas as a hypothesis: stake out a claim that a specific person is stuck on a specific project, then test whether they try to buy before any product exists.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Turns idea selection into fast falsifiable tests instead of intuition over a notebook of ideas.

insights.claim: Ideas should come from firsthand immersion, not whiteboard brainstorming or short Zoom interviews; one founder shadowed solar installers, then independent physical therapists for days and even considered buying a PT franchise to see the P&L before spotting a pull.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Earned insight from doing the job beats desk research for finding non-obvious pull.
insights.quote: You would go all out. You would go in person.

insights.claim: Of about 50 companies Snyder has worked with, roughly 10% found their idea through their own experience and 90% by going and gaining firsthand experience with customers, some by selling the wrong product first.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Most successful ideas are discovered externally, so founders need a process for immersion, not just domain expertise.

insights.claim: Solve-your-own-problem works only if you would have paid someone to solve it; the Clearly AI founder, a former AWS security engineer, qualified, whereas things you merely think should exist often fail the mirror test.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Applies a willingness-to-pay filter to the common founder-market-fit heuristic.

insights.claim: The pull hypothesis is validated with two slides: first restate your understanding of their project, urgency and why options fall short, aiming for an 'oh my god, yes'; then a conceptual outline of how you can help.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Gives a low-cost, product-free artifact for pre-build demand tests.

insights.claim: Design partners are an anti-pattern: people who sign up to be design partners give visionary feedback and never buy, while people with an important job to get done just want it done.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Free co-design relationships select against real pull and convert a buying signal into a favor.
insights.quote: you recruit a design partner who quote unquote buys into your vision for the product and they give a bunch of feedback and never buy

insights.claim: Building the product yourself before talking to customers is a major trap; with AI it takes weeks rather than months but you should still face reality as early as possible.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Cheaper building tempts founders to delay the customer conversations that matter.

insights.claim: Tarpit idea: entering a space with a clear winner without a theory of a newly unblocked customer, e.g. cloning a fast-growing bootstrapped sales automation tool, almost always fails, and a merely better product (even a 100x better printer) is not bought by people who are not blocked.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Better-than-incumbent is not a demand signal; blocked customers are.

insights.claim: Cold outreach at the earliest stage should be a short 'founder magic' message that is simply interesting (e.g. 'Snoop Dogg invested in us', a PhD dropout, a former chief of staff) with no pitch, since the only goal is getting a conversation.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Outreach copy optimizes for curiosity, not conversion; pitch templates produce 'leave me alone'.

insights.claim: AI personalization in early outreach doesn't work: it tells prospects what they already know and reads as machine written, and personalization matters little at this stage.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Mass-personalized AI email is not an edge for early customer discovery.

insights.claim: LinkedIn outreach benchmarks: add 100-150 people per week, expect 30-40% to accept, 30-50% of those to reply, and most repliers to agree to a call; low acceptance points to the profile, low replies to the message.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Provides diagnostics to tell which part of the top of funnel is broken.

insights.claim: Snyder aims for two to three prospect conversations per day, with 30-minute calendar blocks because shorter ones are overlooked and lead to no-shows.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Sets a cadence benchmark for founder-led discovery.

insights.claim: Call structure: ask why they took the call (often they fill in the pull framework for you), agree an agenda, ask permission to ask context questions, then probe project, urgency, options and limitations; the pitch is a small restatement, not a product vision.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Concrete script that keeps discovery from feeling like interrogation and avoids over-pitching.

insights.claim: If you feel you are pushing or convincing on a call, that is a red flag; real pull looks like 'wait, you can do what? How do we get started?' while lukewarm enthusiasm like 'send more info' or 'Q4' is a pushed-out-into-the-future non-signal.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Distinguishes pull-shaped actions from polite interest in pipeline reviews.
insights.quote: a pull-shaped action is like I need this right now.

insights.claim: The Hail Mary question, 'is there anything on your to-do list you would pay me to do right now?', has repeatedly redirected startups; an applicant tracking startup selling to governments got its first customer from a job-description task.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Open-ended ask can reveal adjacent paid work when the hypothesis is wrong.

insights.claim: After about five calls review whether any pull was found; a startup with five flat banking calls got an intro to defense companies where the reaction was immediate, prompting a new hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: A short check-in cadence prevents both premature pivots and endless calls without learning.

insights.claim: Close early deals by restating the pull in a small concept and returning with a rough mockup (a pharma founder vibe-coded one in days with no slides) rather than building first or offering pilots, proofs of concept or free design partnerships.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Speed to a concrete concept converts pull before it cools.

insights.claim: Pull framework sets price bounds: the value of getting the project done and the cost of the alternatives (e.g. $50,000/year paid to market research consultants) give an intuitive anchor.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Anchors pricing on the buyer's current spend rather than founder cost-plus.

insights.claim: Early on test willingness to transact over willingness to pay; when higher pricing matters, present a semi-real case study range (e.g. $80,000 to $1 million) and ask the buyer to react rather than proposing a number.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Case-study anchoring lets buyer and seller jointly react to a number without a confrontation.

insights.claim: For larger deals, ask the champion when results must show (e.g. Q1) and work backwards as a forcing function for every sales step.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Aligns enterprise sales process to the buyer's own deadline.

insights.claim: Service-shaped early delivery, where humans do the work behind an AI product while pull is validated, can work despite the risk of becoming a low-margin consultancy, with AI gradually automating more.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Services-as-software is a viable wedge to learn what to automate.

insights.claim: Post-sale, every customer is guaranteed to churn until some X after which it is weird to churn; the job is finding X (not usage or NPS; e.g. Slack's message-count threshold) and designing onboarding so every customer reaches it.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Retention is engineered via a leading indicator, not hoped for.
insights.quote: everybody who buys is guaranteed to churn until X in which case they're weird to churn

insights.claim: A horizontal AI workflows startup with 90%+ churn found that freight forwarders retained using one workflow, then pivoted to a premium freight-forwarder product.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Mining the retained minority for pull is a path out of horizontal-product churn.

insights.claim: A startup is a factory that repeats one case study (they were trying X, existing options failed for Y, we offered Z) in which customers say hell yes before and after buying; the stages are pipeline, sales and delivery.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Simplifies the startup into one repeatable unit so effort targets a single pipeline.

insights.claim: Apply the theory of constraints to the case study factory: find the single bottleneck (pipeline, close rate, retention), fix it, then move to the next.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Gives a prioritization rule for where a seed-stage team should spend time.

insights.claim: Fast-growing AI startups are finding pockets of pull where buyers instantly pull the product out; Snyder saw an enterprise deal close in about two weeks versus 18 months historically.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Stronger pull compresses sales cycles dramatically, implying cycle length is a pull diagnostic.

insights.claim: Pull analysis explains why Linear-style better-UX wins only if some user is blocked by the incumbent's experience; Snyder tried 'better UX' in HR software and failed because UX was not relevant to the buyer.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Better UX is a wedge only when the buyer is blocked by the existing experience.

insights.claim: Mature companies can use the same approach for a second product: sell new features to existing customers before building; one leader said every idea that came from customer asks in sales calls worked and every whiteboarded one failed.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Customer-pull-sourced roadmaps beat internal ideation in incumbents.

insights.claim: When stuck, 'goblin mode' (e.g. scheduling 20 meetings at a conference, a founder's parents knocking door to door on dental offices for Tiro) is a break-glass tactic to get customers in front of you quickly to form a new hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Rob Snyder
insights.so_what: Short bursts of extreme customer exposure can unstick a zero-to-one search.
